children: The U.S. Gulf Coast diesel crack spread—the premium refiners earn turning crude into diesel—broke above $100 a barrel in August, the first time that gauge has ever reached triple digits.
In ordinary conditions it trades between $15 and $30. Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok argues the spike is not a fleeting energy-line item. It is a core inflation shock.

Gasoline surges mainly tax household driving and other discretionary spending. Diesel is different. It is an intermediate input baked into the delivered cost of almost every physical good: trucking and rail freight, farm machinery, construction equipment, and the logistics that move inventory.
When that fuel becomes unusually expensive relative to crude, the extra cost does not remain confined to the energy component of the CPI. With a lag, it migrates into core goods and services.

That delayed pass-through is precisely the kind of inflation the Federal Reserve cannot treat as transitory. Slok’s conclusion is that diesel margins are now helping set the long end of the Treasury curve, because the crack spread itself has become an important leading indicator of future core inflation.

Soft crude prices can therefore understate the pressure still working through the industrial economy. As inventories stay tight and global refining capacity remains constrained, that channel is likely to stay relevant for policymakers and bond markets alike.

title: Diesel’s record refining premium is feeding core inflation, Apollo warns
